items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the integral
[MATH: \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}]

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4x^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
As it is, this integral doesn't resemble any of the basic integrals we have encountered so far. However, we can rewrite our integral as

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4x^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}x = 2 \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(2x\right)^2-1}}\textrm{d}x,]

Content:
which becomes very similar to the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

Content:
[MATH: \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcosh u+C.]

Content:
The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: 2x.]

Content:
So, let [MATH: u=2x.] Differentiating, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2} \,\textrm{d}u.]

Content:
Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and compute it, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(2)/(sqrt(4x^{2} − 1))dx|= 2∫(1)/(sqrt((2x)^{2} − 1))dx; = 2∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1)) ⋅ (1)/(2)du; = ∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1))du; = arcosh u + C; = arcosh (2x) + C]

EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: ewcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{ m arsinh} olimits} ewcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{ m arcosh} olimits} ewcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{ m artanh} olimits} ewcommand{\sech}{\mathop{ m sech} olimits} ewcommand{\csch}{\mathop{ m csch} olimits} ewcommand{\coth}{\mathop{ m coth} olimits} ewcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{ m arsech} olimits} ewcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{ m arcsch} olimits} ewcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{ m arcoth} olimits}]

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

[MATH: \int rac{1}{\sqrt{u^2+1}}\, extrm{d}u = \arsinh u+C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u^2] as the variable, we have [MATH: 2x^2 = \left(\sqrt{2}\,x ight)^2.]

So, let's substitute [MATH: u =\sqrt{2}\,x.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{ extrm{d}u}{ extrm{d}x}=\sqrt{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad extrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \, extrm{d}u.]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and compute it, as follows:

[MATH: ∫(π)/(sqrt(2x^{2} + 1))dx|= ∫(π)/(sqrt((sqrt(2)x)^{2} + 1))dx; = π∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1)) ⋅ ((1)/(sqrt(2))du); = (π)/(sqrt(2))∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1))du; = (π)/(sqrt(2))arsinh u + C; = (π)/(sqrt(2))arsinh (sqrt(2)x) + C]

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: ewcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{ m arsinh} olimits} ewcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{ m arcosh} olimits} ewcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{ m artanh} olimits} ewcommand{\sech}{\mathop{ m sech} olimits} ewcommand{\csch}{\mathop{ m csch} olimits} ewcommand{\coth}{\mathop{ m coth} olimits} ewcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{ m arsech} olimits} ewcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{ m arcsch} olimits} ewcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{ m arcoth} olimits}]

Let's rewrite our integral as

[MATH: \int \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x^2-4}}\, extrm{d}x = \dfrac{3}{2} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left( rac{x}{2} ight)^2-1}} \, extrm{d}x.]

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

[MATH: \int rac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, extrm{d}u = \arcosh u+C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u^2] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{x}{2} ight)^2.]

So, let's substitute [MATH: u = \dfrac x 2.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{ extrm{d}u}{ extrm{d}x}= \dfrac{1}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad extrm{d}x =2\, extrm{d}u.]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and evaluate it, as follows: [MATH: ∫(3)/(sqrt(x^{2} − 4))dx|= (3)/(2)∫(1)/(sqrt(((x)/(2))^{2} − 1))dx; = (3)/(2)∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1)) ⋅ 2du; = 3∫(du)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1)); = 3arcosh u + C; = 3arcosh ((x)/(2)) + C]

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

[MATH: \int rac{1}{1-u^2} \, extrm{d}u =\artanh u +C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u^2] as the variable, we have [MATH: 4x^2 = \left(2x ight)^2.]

So, let's substitute [MATH: u=2x.] Differentiating, we get

[MATH: \dfrac{ extrm{d}u}{ extrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2\, extrm d u = extrm d x.]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and evaluate it, as follows:

[MATH: ∫(10)/(1 − 4x^{2})dx|= 10∫(1)/(1 − (2x)^{2})dx; = 10∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ (1)/(2)du; = 5∫(1)/(1 − u^{2})du; = 5artanh u + C; = 5artanh 2x + C]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|2x ight| < 1.]

Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle{\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, extrm{d}x}.]
EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}]

Note that we can rewrite this integral as [MATH: \int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine, [MATH: \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u = \arcosh{u}+C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u^2] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac {x}{2} \right)^2.]

So, let's substitute [MATH: u = \dfrac {x}{2}.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from [MATH: x] to [MATH: u.] [MATH: x|4|2sqrt(5); u|2|sqrt(5)] Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and evaluate: [MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \cdot (2 \, \textrm{d}u) \[5pt] &= \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \[5pt] &= \arcosh u \Big|_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \[5pt] &= \arcosh{\sqrt 5} - \arcosh{2} \[5pt] &= \ln\left(\sqrt 5 + \sqrt{\left(\sqrt 5\right)^2 - 1}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{\left(2\right)^2 - 1}\right) \[5pt] &= \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{5}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) \[5pt] & = \ln\left(\dfrac{2 + \sqrt{5}}{2 + \sqrt{3}} \right) }]

[MATH: \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

Note that we can rewrite this integral as
[MATH: \int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine,
[MATH: \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u = \arcosh{u}+C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u^2] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac {x}{2} \right)^2.]

So, let's substitute [MATH: u = \dfrac {x}{2}.] Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from [MATH: x] to [MATH: u.]
[MATH: x|4|2sqrt(5); u|2|sqrt(5)]
Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and evaluate:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \cdot (2 \, \textrm{d}u) \[5pt]

&= \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh u \Big|_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh{\sqrt 5} - \arcosh{2} \[5pt]

&= \ln\left(\sqrt 5 + \sqrt{\left(\sqrt 5\right)^2 - 1}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{\left(2\right)^2 - 1}\right) \[5pt]

&= \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{5}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) \[5pt]

& = \ln\left(\dfrac{2 + \sqrt{5}}{2 + \sqrt{3}} \right)

}]
